faq: What latitude is the Arctic Circle?
66.5633°N — 90° minus the axial tilt. It drifts roughly 15 m a year as the tilt changes, which is why old roadside signs sit slightly off.
Inside or outside the line — does it say?
Yes: the result's framing tells you which side of the line your point sits on (for circles and tropics, poleward versus equatorward; for the meridian, east versus west).
The shortest surface distance to the line — for latitude lines that is the meridian arc; for the prime meridian it is the great-circle route to the nearest point of the meridian.
Does terrain or sea level matter?
No — distances are surface geometry on the reference sphere; mountains do not shorten the way to a latitude line.
Stand on the line and it is: the tropics and circles have real ground you can occupy, and the result honours it.
Sphere-accurate to well under a kilometre for these magnitudes — plenty for education, planning and curiosity; geodesists refine with the ellipsoid.
Signs and hemispheres are handled — a southern point measures to southern lines by the same geometry.
